(herein appellant) of the offending car.
5. Learned Tribunal vide its judgment and award dated 30.04.2010 found that the accident had
occurred due to rash and negligent driving by respondent No. 3 and awarded compensation of Rs.

17,53,800/ to claimants. The Tribunal foisted liability of paying the compensation on the appellant.
6. In assessing the compensation, learned Tribunal on appreciation of evidence found that the
deceased was a Government servant serving as Manager QC in the Food Corporation of India. His
monthly salary was Rs. 24,149/. He was aged 54 years as at the time of his death. Learned Tribunal
deducted 1/3rd of the salary towards personal expenses of the deceased and took the remaining Rs.
16,100/ as his monthly contribution towards the claimants. Annual contribution of the deceased
towards the claimants thus came out as Rs. 1, 93,200/, which became the 'multiplicand' for
calculating compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'. On the basis of the age of the
deceased, applicable multiplier being 11, learned Tribunal scaled it down to 9. Compensation under
this head thus amounting to Rs. 17, 38, 800/ (1, 93,200x9). In addition, learned Tribunal awarded
Rs. 15,000/ as compensation for funeral expenses. Total compensation thus awarded was Rs. 17,
53,800/.
7. Appellant-Insurance Company has impugned the judgment and award of the learned Tribunal to
the extent of the quantum of compensation awarded to the claimants. Award has been assailed on
the ground that only respondent No. 2, who is a MBA student, should have been taken as dependent
of the deceased, whereas respondent No. 1 could not have been because he is gainfully employed as
per the evidence available before the Tribunal. It is also contended that as per the evidence, the
basic salary of the deceased was Rs. 10,600/ and the total amount which he was drawing after
deduction was Rs. 19,481/. It is also contended that both the claimants were major but this aspect
was ignored by the learned Tribunal.
8. Mr. C. S.

d Tribunal as
claimants' witness. In cross-examination he has admitted that his brother Harpreet Singh is
employed as a clerk in Doordarshan. This aspect is not disputed by the claimants. Appellant in its
objections before the learned Tribunal had clearly contended that the claimants were major and

earning hands. No evidence, however, has been led by the claimants to prove that even claimant
Harpreet Singh was an unemployed person and dependent upon the deceased up to the time of his
death. Since claimant, Harpreet Singh is gainfully employed in a Central Government service and
there is nothing in the claimants' evidence that he was dependent upon the deceased as at the time
of latter's death, appellant's contention that claimant Harpreet Singh cannot be taken as a person
dependent upon the deceased is to be accepted.
11. Viewed thus, correctness of compensation awarded under the head 'loss of dependency' by the
learned Tribunal calls for reconsideration. It needs to be determined, whether claimant, Harpreet
Singh, is entitled to the compensation under this head?
12. Before taking up the above aspect, I will however, first take up the appellant's challenge to the
correctness of the income of the deceased as taken by the learned Tribunal. In this regard, evidence
available with and relied upon by the learned Tribunal is the salary certificate Ex.PW KA issued by
Manager (Accounts), Food Corporation of India, District Office, Jammu. In this certificate, basic pay
of the deceased is shown as Rs. 10,600/ and total salary, inclusive of allowances as Rs. 24,149/.
Deduction towards CPF is shown as Rs. 4352/, Rs. 306/ is shown as deduction towards licensing fee
and Rs. 10/ towards BF. Learned Tribunal, therefore, cannot be said to have erred in taking total
salary of the deceased as Rs. 24,149/ because nothing except income tax paid on the total salary is
deductible, while ascertaining the contribution of the deceased towards his dependents.
13.

say Rs. 1,37,400/ each (half of Rs. 2,74,788/) each. This would be the 'multiplicand' in this case.
26. Deceased at the time of death was in the age group of 50 to 55. Applicable multiplier as per Sarla
Verma's case (supra) is 11. Having regard to the age of the deceased and age of the
dependent-claimant, learned Tribunal can be said to have correctly scaled down the multiplier to

27. Compensation payable under the head 'loss of dependency' would be Rs. 12,36,600/- (1,37,400 x

28. For the aforementioned, this appeal is found to have merit and is, therefore, allowed. Impugned

payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Pilot Court) Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
payload.holding: The Tribunal held the insurance company liable to pay compensation to the three injured claimants after deducting 50% for contributory negligence due to driving without a license and helmets.
payload.ratio: In motor accident claim cases under Section 166 of the MV Act, the standard of proof is based on preponderance of probabilities, and police record documents such as the FIR and charge sheet are sufficient to establish negligence in the absence of rebuttal. Furthermore, contributory negligence is established when the injured rider is proven to have been driving without a valid driving license and without wearing a helmet.

payload.title: Shivlal And Ors. Etc. vs Smt. Rukmabai And Ors.
payload.court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal Ratlam / Madhya Pradesh High Court
payload.holding: The High Court held that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation for the death of a gratuitous passenger carried in a goods vehicle, dismissed the owners' appeal regarding negligence and quantum, and dismissed the claimants' cross-objections for enhancement.
payload.ratio: Where a passenger travelling in a goods vehicle is a gratuitous passenger whose risk is not statutorily required to be covered under Section 95 of the Motor Vehicles Act and is not covered by the terms of the insurance policy, the insurer cannot be held liable for compensation.

19. The contract of insurance in this case was as per terms and conditions embodied in Ex. D-1.
Thereunder the accident tractor was to be used only under a public carrier's permit under the Act.
The policy expressly prohibits use of the vehicle for conveyance of passengers for hire or reward and
in consideration of additional premium covers the risk of only two categories of the employees of the
insured. It may also be pointed out that under Section 96(2)(b)(i) of the Act the insurance company
is entitled to avoid its liability if the vehicle is used in contravention of specified condition of the
permit.

103) where this Court holding that the contract of employment occurring in proviso (ii) to Section
95(1)(b) of the Act need not necessarily be with the insured alone, held the insurer liable where the
death of a labourer of the hirer of the truck had taken place while being carried in the truck. In this
connection the decisions in Abdul Razak's case 1984 Acc a 44 : (AIR 1983 All 400) and Ramesh
Kumar's case AIR 1979 Madh Pra 124 are also pertinent.

the instant case, the deceased Laxminarayan cannot be said to be travelling in the tractor by reason

tractor or had goods to take care of. Therefore, the ratio of the decision in Patharibai's case (supra)

amount of compensation which appears to it to be just. The provision has a wider ambit than the

damages cannot be arrived at by any precise mathematical calculation. It has rightly been observed
that in the assessment of compensation arithmetic is a good servant but a bad master. Fall in the
purchasing power of ruppe has also to be kept in view in determining the amount of compensation.

i.e. the multiplicand and the number of years' purchase i.e. the multiplier and it was adopted in this
Court's decision in State of M.P. v. Devi Ramat, 1981 Jab LJ 42 : (AIR 1981 Madh Pra 173).

"Rule 111(1). Save in the eases of a vehicle which is being used for the carriage of
police (public?) or a stage carriage in which goods are being carried in addition to
passengers no person shall be carried in goods vehicle other than a bona fide
employee of the owner or the hirer of the vehicle, or the owner or the hirer and except
in accordance with this rule."

Section 95(2) of the Act. The policy taken to cover the required minimum is generally referred to as

an Act policy. The law does not require that contract of insurance as respects goods vehicle must

payload.court: In The High Court Of Punjab & Haryana At Chandigarh
payload.holding: The criminal revision petition is partly allowed by upholding the conviction of the petitioner under Sections 279, 337, 304-A, and 427 of the IPC, but modifying the substantive sentence for the offence under Section 304-A IPC from two years of rigorous imprisonment to 18 months, while maintaining the other sentences and fine.
payload.ratio: In-court identification by eyewitnesses is valid and admissible in law even without a prior Test Identification Parade, provided the witnesses had sufficient opportunity to observe the accused. Furthermore, discontinuation of medical treatment or shifting hospitals by a victim does not break the causal link between the accident injuries and death unless supported by medical evidence showing improper care or material alteration of treatment.

args.question: What precedents could the insurance company use AGAINST our client, where the driver had no valid licence? Assess how damaging each one is.

supporting.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
supporting.principle: Where the driver had a fake driving licence, the insurer must pay third-party compensation and then recover from the insured (pay-and-recover).
supporting.fact_alignment: This is the leading Supreme Court authority on fake/no-licence cases. It establishes that even where the driver had no valid licence, the insurer must still pay third-party claimants and then recover from the owner.
supporting.why_it_matters: This is the strongest authority FOR our client (the claimant) — it mandates pay-and-recover, meaning the insurer cannot walk away. The insurer will try to distinguish it or argue it doesn't apply, but this is binding law.
supporting.quote: In case of third-party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount, and if so advised, to recover the same from the insured.

supporting.title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Subbraya
supporting.principle: Where the driver had no valid driving licence, the insurer is liable to pay third-party compensation and then recover from the owner (pay-and-recover), following Swaran Singh and Laxmi Narain Dhut.
supporting.fact_alignment: Directly on point — driver without valid licence. The court applied pay-and-recover, protecting the third-party claimant.
supporting.why_it_matters: Reinforces the binding position that third-party claimants are protected even when the driver had no licence.
supporting.quote: The insurance company is liable to pay the compensation to the claimants and thereafter recover the same from the owner of the vehicle.

supporting.title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
supporting.principle: An insurer has a statutory liability to pay compensation to third parties even if there is a breach of policy conditions (such as an invalid driving licence), and is entitled to recover the same from the insured.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver held a licence for LMV (non-transport) but was driving a goods vehicle (commercial) — breach of policy conditions. Court applied pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Strong authority that even where the driver had the wrong class of licence, the insurer must pay the third party first.
supporting.quote: Even if a conscious breach on the part of the insured is established, still the insurer has a statutory liability to pay the compensation to the third party and will simply have the right to recover the same from the insured/tortfeasor.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V.Vijayakumar
supporting.principle: Where the driver of a transport vehicle holds only a light motor vehicle licence without the specific authorisation or badge required to drive a transport vehicle, there is a breach of policy conditions, but the insurer must pay the third-party compensation first and subsequently recover from the insured owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver had an LMV licence but no badge/authorisation for a transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab). Court applied pay-and-recover.
supporting.why_it_matters: Strong authority that even where the driver had a licence but for the wrong class of vehicle, the insurer must still pay the third party first.
supporting.quote: The doctrine of 'pay and recover' has been recognised by the Supreme Court in several decisions.

supporting.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar
supporting.principle: Where the driver had no valid driving licence, the insurer is liable to pay third-party compensation and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver without valid licence — pay-and-recover applied.
supporting.why_it_matters: Consistent application of the Swaran Singh framework protecting third-party claimants.

supporting.title: National Insurance Company Ltd vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
supporting.principle: Where the driver had no valid driving licence, the insurer is liable to pay third-party compensation and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver without valid licence — pay-and-recover applied.
supporting.why_it_matters: Consistent application of the Swaran Singh framework protecting third-party claimants.

supporting.title: The Manager vs Chennamma
supporting.principle: Where the driver had no valid driving licence, the insurer is liable to pay third-party compensation and then recover from the owner.
supporting.fact_alignment: Driver without valid licence — pay-and-recover applied.
supporting.why_it_matters: Consistent application of the Swaran Singh framework protecting third-party claimants.

adverse.title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
adverse.principle: A fake driving licence constitutes a fundamental breach of policy conditions, entitling the insurer to recover from the insured after paying third parties.
adverse.risk_to_client: The insurer will argue that a fake/no licence is a 'fundamental breach' that shifts the ultimate financial burden to the owner. While the insurer must still pay the claimant, they will seek recovery from the owner, which could leave our client (if they are the owner) exposed to a recovery suit.
adverse.distinguishing_argument: This case actually supports pay-and-recover — the insurer must pay the claimant first. The risk is only to the owner (if our client is the owner), not to the third-party claimant. If our client is the claimant, this case HELPS us.

strategy.compensation_reasoning: Compensation will be computed under the Sarla Verma / Pranay Sethi framework regardless of the licence issue. The licence defect affects who pays (insurer vs owner), not the quantum.
risks: If the deceased/claimant was a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle or private vehicle, the insurer may argue complete exoneration under Sukumarbai (doc_028), Minor Mahesh Kanubhai (doc_029), or Shivlal (doc_014) — this is the HIGHEST risk.
